title: Screen Time and AI Need Different Questions
author: Steve Karandy
summary: Steve Karandy, a school tech director and parent, argues that schools are damaging the debate by folding screen time and AI into a single question about devices. Screen time concerns exposure, sleep, movement and what the time replaces, while AI raises separate questions about who is doing the thinking, accuracy, authorship and student data. He takes screen concerns seriously, citing the American Academy of Pediatrics' 2026 policy and a short Danish family trial, but notes that neither tested classroom laptops or AI. On AI he cites an Education Endowment Foundation trial of the Aila planning tool, which cut teacher preparation time by about 24 percent without a quality penalty, and a high-school maths experiment in which an unguarded AI tool improved assisted practice but hurt later unassisted performance. He admits the two issues overlap, since chatbots can prolong screen use and AI can become a shortcut around thinking. He closes with five planning questions on learning goal, what is replaced, what thinking stays with the student, safeguards and evidence for changing course.
points: Screen time and AI are different policy questions: one is about exposure and displacement, the other about who does the thinking, accuracy, authorship and privacy.
Teacher-facing AI use can be judged on its own, as in the EEF Aila trial where preparation time fell about 24 percent with no quality loss, though that is not evidence of better student learning.
A 2025 maths experiment found an open-ended AI tool raised assisted performance but lowered later unassisted results, so better-looking work is not the same as stronger understanding.
Review every activity from both directions, its effect on time and attention and its effect on thinking, responsibility and safety, because the concerns can coexist in one lesson.
Before adopting a tool, ask five questions: what learning goal requires it, what it replaces, what thinking stays with the student, what safeguards fit, and what evidence would change course.
quotes: The screen-time conversation asks how much time children spend with media, what they encounter, and what that time replaces. The AI conversation also asks who is doing the thinking, whether information is accurate, whose work is being presented, and what happens to student data.

When we collapse those questions into one argument about devices, we make it harder to address either well. A limit on screen minutes cannot tell us whether a student understands an AI-assisted answer.

A school should be able to explain why a digital activity deserves students’ time. Calling something educational does not automatically make it worthwhile. Nor does an engaging app earn unlimited access to the school day.

Consider a teacher using AI to generate possible discussion questions, then checking and adapting them before a device-free seminar. The teacher has used AI. Students have not added a minute of screen exposure.

A 2025 high-school mathematics experiment makes the distinction concrete. Students using an open-ended AI tool performed better during assisted practice but worse on a later unassisted assessment than students without it.
Better-looking work and stronger understanding are different outcomes. We need to check both.
What does it replace? A ten-minute activity may be reasonable on its own and still add to a day already crowded with screens.
We owe families a clearer explanation than being for or against screens. We owe students opportunities to learn with useful tools and opportunities to learn without them.
